newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: OPINION - Chilanga Cement div cheers Zambia bourse.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Chilanga Cement div cheers Zambia bourse.

text.p: By Charles Mate, Lusaka Stock Exchange general manager

Chilanga Cement Plc announced its 1996 financial results on Thursday 20 February 1997 and completely surprised many by its strong performance. Most notable was the proposed final dividend of seven kwacha a share against two kwacha in 1995. Based on the recent 1996 financial results the earnings per share of 17.59 kwacha gives the stock a historic profit/earnings ratio (PE) of 3.24 down from 12.81. This PE is lower than that of Zambia Sugar Plc at 4.75.
Almost everyone has welcomed these results -- and many would say this is the sort of performance the stock badly needed to regain its attraction and appeal.

For many Zambians Chilanga Cement represents their first taste and exposure to the stock market. Chilanga Cement was floated and listed on the newly established Lusaka Stock Exchange in May 1995 in a mood of high expectations and excitement about Zambia's privatisation process. In Zambia's first ever public flotation, thousands of Zambians were given the opportunity to own shares for the first time. In terms of the objectives of economic empowerment and encouraging wide share ownership, the Chilanga flotation was hugely successful.

Chilanga increased the number of its shareholders from around 450 mostly non-Zambians to around 4,750 shareholders as a result of the floatation. A total of 54,750,970 shares (27.4 percent of the total equity) was offered at 65 kwacha a share (US $0.07). The offer was fully subscribed.

After the listing on 22 May 1995, almost everyone expected the share price to rise. Active trading in the secondary market was premised on the belief that there would be significant interest by foreign investors. It was thought that foreign investors, being more well informed and more sophisticated, would notice the strong correlation between Chilanga's prospects and a privatised mining industry, in particular the Konkola Deep Mining Project (KDMP) seen as the backbone to the viability and continuity of the Zambian copper mines and the economy. The prospectus had disclosed Chilanga's strategic positioning in relation to KDMP.

The awaited and expected stampede by foreign investors into Chilanga Cement did not materialise. A major deterrent to serious foreign interest was the sudden weakening of the domestic currency from 816 kwacha to the dollar in April to 950 kwacha by December 1995 and 1,240 kwacha by May 1996 -- a fifty percent drop in the 12 months after the listing.

The share price rose briefly after the listing on 22 May from 65 kwacha to 68 kwacha by August and then began to fall. By December 1995 the share price had dropped by ten percent to 58 kwacha. At this stage, many claimed the offer had been overpriced - and hence the decline in the share price.

As if that was not enough, the dividend for 1995 of two kwacha a share did not find much enthusiasm with many new small shareholders. This dividend became an intractable debating issue. The situation was further polarised by the lack of a developed financial press for serious analysis of the issues and the vacuum was largely filled by sensationalism. The point was completely missed by many commentators and new shareholders that the management team at Chilanga had been in office for less than a year and was in the process of a major reorganisation and review of market opportunities.

The management of Chilanga Cement responded admirably to these problems in the early part of 1996, with a great sense of commitment to the new shareholders, as well as the information disclosure requirements of a listed company. In collaboration with the stock exchange, the company sent a letter to each and every shareholder explaining the nature of share investment, dividends, benefits and risks as well as information to help first time investors understand their investment.
Two years later and with the announcement of the impressive 1996 results many believe Chilanga Cement has been transformed.
Chilanga provides many useful lessons for policy makers and decision managers on privatisation issues and the creation of related stock markets.

The pricing of the first initial public offer on a new stock exchange is obviously important and critical for the success of the newly established stock market and to engender the support of the general public to the concepts of privatisation and share ownership. But what is the best price? In particular, what is the best price in a privatised flotation with the multiple objectives of wide share ownership and jump starting the stock exchange?
Clearly the issue is even more complicated where the offer price also encompasses a revenue generation motive for the government.

Firstly, it is interesting to discover and note that in a start up market the PE ratio may not have significant relevance or bearing on the behaviour of new investors and hence share price movement in the secondary market. For example, a PE as low as two does not necessarily guarantee that the price will rise after the listing. Standard and conventional performance indicators such as PE have little immediate impact on the behaviour of first time investors whose main motive is the notion of owning a share of the nation's assets.

Whilst the price is obviously an important factor, an interesting observation is that the success of a flotation will be heavily influenced by the type of new investor, in particular their liquidity demands and degree of knowledge between short term and long term investment.

Secondly the price of Chilanga Cement did not drop from 65 kwacha to 50 kwacha because the fundamentals of the company had deteriorated. To the contrary, Chilanga had in the Commonwealth Development Corporation (CDC) a new strong management and major shareholder committed to growth and profitability. The price dropped largely because many of the new investors were desperate for cash -- and the only avenue open to them to obtain this liquidity was by lowering their offer prices to cash out and exit the market. Such liquidity demands were driven by pressures such as payment of electricity bills, school fees etc...

This problem can easily be corrected by raising the participation threshold whilst maintaining a low price. For example Zambia Sugar Plc was offered in August 1996 at 11 kwacha a share but in parcels of 10,000 shares only, whereas Chilanga was available to entry levels of 1,000 shares and in multiples of 100 shares thereafter. Zambia Sugar has seen a steady gradual share price rise from 11 kwacha to 14 kwacha six months after the listing -- a rise of 27 percent.

Thirdly, teaching new investors that shares should be viewed as a long term investment is a difficult proposition in an environment where everyone is focused on short-term immediate gains. To succeed and win support, a new stock market needs some dose of a "feel good" factor.
The dividends paid by the company should reflect this. A dividend-based valuation approach may therefore be particularly relevant and apt for a new start up market.

Fourthly, companies are often not adequately prepared for the extra demands placed on them by their new shareholders and the media. The resultant lack of information, and cooperation from the company leads to mistrust, frustration and lack of confidence all which can cause shareholders to want out.
Chilanga Cement as the pioneer listing on the bourse has responded positively to the challenges it has faced both in its business operations as well as its accountability to the market place.
The 1996 results place Chilanga on a pedestal of higher expectations in 1997. For now, in only two years of operating as a listed company, Chilanga appears to have delivered.
Over the next months it will be interesting to note how the market responds and the lessons that will emerge as the Zambian stock market firms up.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
